hooks.text: Great white sharks don't actually want to eat you.
Most great white shark bites are simply curiosity.
Great white sharks have three hundred active teeth.

title: Why Great White Sharks Rarely Eat Humans
description: Discover the surprising science behind great white shark bites and why humans are not on their menu.

beats.text: Great white sharks don't actually want to eat you.
emphasis: don't actually want to eat you
beats.visual: Great white shark swimming underwater, Carcharodon carcharias

beats.text: For many decades, Hollywood movies and popular novels cemented the great white shark as a relentless man-eater.
beats.visual: Historical scientific illustration of a white shark, Carcharodon carcharias

beats.text: Marine scientists explain that most recorded bites are actually exploratory investigations by curious animals.
beats.visual: Shark researcher underwater studying marine life

beats.text: When encountering an unfamiliar object like a surfboard, the massive apex predator takes a careful test bite.
beats.visual: Close up of great white shark teeth, Carcharodon carcharias jaw

beats.text: It uses flexible tooth beds and sensitive jaws to gather tactile evidence and figure out what is floating there.
beats.visual: Shark lateral line anatomy diagram and sensory organs illustration

beats.text: Because human bodies are much too bony and completely lack high-fat blubber, sharks almost always spit us straight back out.
beats.visual: Seal swimming in the ocean as natural prey, Arctocephalus pusillus
